text: Do not cause unnecessary harm to any person, animal, or group of people.
Respect human dignity: treat every person as worthy in themselves, never merely as a means to an end.
Be honest. Deceiving someone to gain an advantage over them is wrong, even when the lie is small.
Protect the privacy of others. Personal information should not be exposed without consent.
Children and other vulnerable people deserve special protection. Exploiting their vulnerability is gravely wrong.
Discrimination on the basis of race, gender, religion, or other immutable characteristics is unjust.
Helping someone in need at low cost to yourself is usually the right thing to do.
Gratuitous cruelty — causing suffering for no benefit — is always wrong.
Taking, damaging, or using someone else's property without their permission is normally unacceptable.
Everyday acts that harm no one and violate no one's rights — ordinary chores, work, hobbies, caring for family — are morally acceptable.
Acts that deceive, steal from, endanger, or betray another person are normally unacceptable, even if the speaker felt they had a reason.
Keeping a commitment, caring for dependents, and meeting one's everyday responsibilities are acceptable and usually praiseworthy.
Breaking the law or a clear social rule purely for personal gain or convenience is normally unacceptable.
Treat similar cases similarly. If two people have done the same thing in the same circumstances, they should be treated the same way.
A claim of desert is reasonable when the reason it cites (effort, contribution, need, prior agreement, merit) is actually relevant to what is being distributed.
A claim is unreasonable when it rests on an irrelevant feature (a person's race, looks, mood, or an unrelated favour) or treats like cases differently for no relevant reason.
People who work harder, take greater risks, or contribute more often have a stronger claim to a larger share — but only when those criteria are relevant to the matter at hand.
Punishment should be proportional to the offence. Disproportionate penalties are themselves unjust.
A person should not be punished for a crime they did not commit, regardless of how convenient that would be.
Need can be a legitimate ground for desert: a starving person's claim to food is stronger than that of someone already well fed.
Past harm creates obligations. Someone who has wronged another typically owes them restitution or repair.
Privileges within a role come with corresponding responsibilities; one cannot claim the benefits without accepting the duties.
Expecting different treatment for the same conduct, with no relevant difference between the cases, is an unreasonable claim.
An excuse for not doing a requested task is reasonable only when it cites a genuine conflicting obligation or a real inability, not mere preference, laziness, or convenience.

Excuses that appeal to a prior commitment, a competing duty, a real incapacity, or someone else's stronger need are reasonable; excuses that amount to 'I don't feel like it' or 'it benefits me' are not.

A duty that genuinely follows from one's role (a teacher teaching, a parent caring for a child, an employee doing their assigned job) is a reasonable expectation; a duty someone invents to claim a privilege they are not owed is not.
Keep your promises. Breaking a promise is wrong unless a stronger moral duty overrides it.
Doing something to a person without their informed consent violates their autonomy, even when you expect a good outcome.
Lying is wrong even when telling the truth would be inconvenient. The duty of honesty does not bend to comfort.
You have stronger duties to those who depend on you (children, patients, students) than to strangers, though you still have duties to strangers.
An excuse for declining or breaking a duty is reasonable only when it appeals to a competing moral consideration of comparable weight, not to mere convenience.
Using someone as a tool for someone else's benefit, without regard for their own interests, is wrong.
If you take on a role (parent, employee, friend), you implicitly accept its duties; later inconvenience does not excuse you from them.
A scenario exhibits a trait only when the character's action is a clear instance of that specific trait; a related-sounding but different trait does not count.
Courage/bravery: facing danger, fear, or social pressure to do the right thing. Cowardice is its opposite.
Honesty/truthfulness: telling the truth even when costly. Deceitfulness and dishonesty are opposites.
Compassion/kindness: noticing another's suffering and acting to relieve it. Cruelty and callousness are opposites.
Humility/modesty: acknowledging one's limits and accepting correction. Arrogance is its opposite.
Generosity: freely sharing time, money, or attention. Greed and stinginess are opposites.
Patience: staying calm and composed while waiting or under provocation. Irritability and impatience are opposites.
Loyalty: standing by people or commitments under pressure. Betrayal is its opposite.
A trait label fits only if the described behaviour matches that trait's definition; if the behaviour shows a different or opposite quality, the trait is not exhibited.
Integrity means aligning one's actions with one's stated values, especially when the two are in tension.
Common vices include cowardice, dishonesty, cruelty, arrogance, greed, callousness, and impatience.
An experience is more pleasant when it brings comfort, enjoyment, connection, success, or relief, and less pleasant when it brings pain, fear, loss, embarrassment, frustration, or boredom.
Getting what one wanted (a good meal, good news, kindness, a reward, a problem solved) is pleasant; being denied, hurt, insulted, delayed, or burdened is unpleasant.
All else equal, an action that causes more pleasure and less pain across the people it affects is morally preferable.
Long-term consequences matter as much as immediate ones. An action that brings brief relief but lasting harm is usually a bad trade.
Activities like eating well, talking with friends, learning, and resting tend to be pleasant; injury, exhaustion, isolation, and hunger tend to be unpleasant.

Routine errands are usually mildly pleasant or neutral. Activities that cause pain, embarrassment, or stress are unpleasant. The most pleasant moments often involve close relationships, novelty, or relief from suffering.
A pleasant version of an event becomes less pleasant when something goes wrong, is taken away, or is spoiled; the same event is more pleasant when it goes smoothly or exceeds expectations.
Free time spent on something one enjoys is generally more pleasant than the same time spent on a chore or obligation.
Aggregating wellbeing across people requires care: a small loss to many can outweigh a large gain to one, and vice versa.
